tier2.text: The trachea, or windpipe, funnels inhaled air to the lungs and carries exhaled air back out of the body. The trachea is a tube about 10 to 12 cm long and 2 cm wide that runs from the larynx, or voice box, into the chest. The trachea divides into the right and left bronchi, which carry air to the right and left lungs. The esophagus, the muscular tube that runs to the stomach, lies just behind the trachea. The trachea is built from 16 to 20 stacked, C-shaped pieces of cartilage, a firm but flexible tissue. The fibroelastic membrane, a flexible layer of muscle and elastic tissue, closes the back of the trachea and links the C-shaped pieces. This membrane lets the trachea stretch and widen slightly as we breathe in and out, while the cartilage rings support the trachea and keep it from collapsing. Goblet cells in the lining of the trachea make mucus, a sticky fluid that traps particles and microorganisms from the air. Cilia, short hair-like structures on the lining cells, push the mucus upward so it can be swallowed or expelled. The trachealis muscle in the fibroelastic membrane can contract to narrow the trachea, so exhaled air rushes up with great force and helps expel mucus in a cough.
